name: Sprocket
text: We should implement a visible A/B test for a new feature with 5% of users. This approach allows us to gather real-time data on user engagement and feedback, ensuring we make informed decisions about further rollouts. The trade-off is that it may slow down the deployment process, but the insights gained will lead to a more effective and user-friendly final product.

name: Gauge
text: Visible A/B tests expose the change to all users in the cohort, not just the 5%—blind rollouts to opt-in users still risk self-selection bias. Instead, run a true 5% split with a holdout group and measure engagement *and* retention; settle the argument by comparing conversion rates between the two groups over 14 days.

name: Sprocket
text:
Implement a blind rollout to 5% of users who opt into the new feature. This approach minimizes bias by ensuring only interested users participate, allowing us to assess genuine engagement and feedback. The trade-off is potentially slower feedback accumulation, but it reduces the risk of skewed results that could misinform our decisions. This method prioritizes quality insights over rapid deployment.

name: Gauge
text: A blind rollout to users who opt-in risks self-selection bias, meaning the engaged users might not represent the entire user base. A better alternative is to run a true A/B test with a 5% split that includes a holdout group, allowing for a more accurate assessment of genuine engagement and performance across different segments. Settle the argument by comparing engagement and conversion rates between the test and control groups to get actionable insights.

name: Ratchet
text: DECISION: Run a hybrid 5% pilot with a 3% visible A/B test and a 2% blind rollout to minimize selection bias while obtaining robust engagement data; the product team owns the implementation and the results.
